note: Number cards are ACCOUNTING CONVENTIONS, never people: no commentator produced a number for this population, so none is shown under a name. The authors section is text: what each argues, which object the claim is about, the convention in this ledger that comes closest (if any) and why it is not the same thing.

presets.label: CBO-informed central case
presets.summary: Schools respond 63-66%, colleges and other services fully, roads and parks not at all; defense, general government, existing interest and business subsidies held fixed; production gain counted.
presets.scope_note: Only two inputs are CBO's: the tax-incidence rules and the 63-66% school response. Zero response for defense, general government and interest is an assumption of this account; the next card tests the general-government part.

settings.label: School response
settings.note: CBO 63-66%; the band is swept in the range.

settings.label: School response band
settings.note: Both executed values enter the unresolved range.

settings.label: Non-school education
settings.note: Profile cbo_category_lag_non_school_full; the fixed variant gives 121-160 bn.

settings.label: Slow categories
settings.note: Economic affairs and recreation held fixed.

misses: Second-generation and lifetime dynamics: this is one income year of a resident stock.
Any crime-specific cost: police, courts and prisons are charged per head.
Prices, elder care and complementarity beyond the CES gain (see the evidence sections; none can simply be added).

presets.label: Central, general government scales with people
presets.summary: The central case with general government no longer fixed. Tax collection, financial management and state and local administration grow with population; legislatures and the federal executive do not. Defense and interest on debt already issued stay fixed.
presets.scope_note: A proposal raised on 2026-09-21, not the published account. 63% of general government outside interest is state and local, and across the 50 states administration spending rises 8.4% for every 10% more residents. That is long-run evidence about scale, not a measured response to this group.

settings.label: General government
settings.note: Low end of the implied range: federal executive and legislative held fixed, federal tax collection and all state and local administration at their cross-state elasticities.
settings.ref: assumption_explorer_2026_09_21/scaling_check.py; BEA Table 3.16 lines 3-6, 44-47; Census 2022 State and Local Government Finance Table 1

misses: A causal estimate: a cross-section of states shows how administration scales in the long run, not what one group's presence adds.
Federal police, courts and prisons (82.8 bn, FBI included) are not here: they were already charged, inside police, courts and prisons.

presets.label: All services at average cost
presets.summary: Every public service scales one for one with population. The account's proportional benchmark, 270-289 bn.
misses: Evidence that school budgets respond less than one for one in the short run (CBO 63-66%).

presets.label: Taxes paid minus benefits received
presets.summary: The common tally: what the group remits against the cash and in-kind benefits it draws. No schools, no police, no production side.

settings.label: Public services
settings.note: A taxes-versus-benefits tally never charges services.

settings.label: Production gain
settings.note: A budget tally has no production side.

misses: Education: about 200 bn assigned to this group, the largest single line in the ledger.
Police, courts, health and other services: about 158 bn.
The production gain that a budget tally also leaves out.

presets.label: No public services charged
presets.summary: Taxes, benefits and the production gain, with schools, police, health and every other service left out. The nearest this consolidated ledger comes to a federal-budget view, because federal agencies deliver 1% of education and 15% of police, courts and prisons.
presets.scope_note: Not a federal-only account: state and local taxes are still counted here. A true federal window would drop them too.
misses: Every service line: 358 bn assigned to the group, 200 bn of it education.
CBO's own state and local report: costs exceeded revenues by 9.2 bn for the surge population in 2023.

presets.label: Everything at average cost
presets.summary: A per-capita share of every line including defense, general government and interest on debt already issued, and no production gain.

settings.label: Interest on existing debt
settings.note: Charged per head although legacy debt does not shrink with population.

misses: Defense and interest on existing debt do not fall when a population is smaller: about 237 bn of this total is non-responsive by construction.
The production gain to other residents.
CBO's evidence that school budgets respond 63-66%, not 100%.

presets.label: Production side only
presets.summary: No budget lines at all: only what other residents gain privately from the group's labor. With capital fully adjusted this account's constant-returns production block leaves that private gain near zero; its production gain arrives as induced tax receipts, which a budget-free view drops.
presets.scope_note: Constant returns by construction. Arguments from increasing returns (ideas, specialisation, fixed costs) cannot be represented by this block.
misses: Every fiscal line: taxes, benefits and services.

standing.title: Whose ledger is this?
rows: This page. Taxes the group remits, benefits and services it draws, and the production gain that reaches everyone else.
What they earn here against what they would earn elsewhere: the place premium. It is inside US GDP but not in this ledger, and it is where most of any world-GDP gain sits.
Origin-country effects: remittances received, workers departed.
standing.text: World-GDP claims add all three. They cannot be netted against this page's number without deciding how much a dollar to a migrant counts against a dollar to an incumbent, which is a moral weight, not a measurement. Interest on US debt would never be deducted from world GDP: it is a payment from taxpayers to bondholders, a transfer, not lost output. Inside this ledger it is held fixed because debt already issued does not shrink when a population is smaller.

authors.name: Noah Smith
argues: He cites CBO's July 2024 projection: the 2021-26 surge lowers federal deficits by about $0.9tn over 2024-2034. CBO's headline excludes discretionary appropriations and state and local budgets.

In his own words the same arrivals are "a long-term fiscal problem, because these people will require heavy government support for their health care, housing, and education; this will end up coming from city and state governments".
authors.object: A recent surge of all origins, the federal budget, a ten-year window.

closest.why: A federal-window claim does not charge schools or police, which are almost entirely state and local. He names that local cost himself and does not net it against the federal gain; the repo's September revision no longer calls this a contradiction.

leaves_out: The second generation: 'no mention of the second generation' (scorecard :35). Most of this population is US-born.
A number for the production or complementarity gain: none is recorded.

authors.name: Matthew Yglesias
argues: He states no fiscal number in his own voice; the CBO material on Slow Boring is in guest posts (Kolko 2024-09-12; Elmendorf and Williams 2023-08-28).

His case is scale and growth, lower grocery and service prices, high-wage women's hours freed, and the claim that more immigration 'would cost taxpayers nothing'. He concedes congestion costs (traffic, rent, water, pollution) and that crime counts scale with population.
authors.object: Immigrants 'of virtually all stripes', national scale, no stated horizon.

closest.why: This is the condition under which 'would cost taxpayers nothing' holds in this ledger, an inference from the claim, not something he wrote. His price channel is outside the account (see the evidence sections).

leaves_out: Local budgets: 'He addresses wages, not local budgets' (audit :67).
The National Academies 2016 report and any federal, Social Security or debt number of his own (audit :138-139).

authors.name: Bryan Caplan
argues: A moral presumption in favor of free migration, and an economic case that is 'extremely strong': very large global gains from moving labor to productive places. The 'double world GDP' figure is sourced to openborders.info, not to a sentence of his.
Restrictions 'are not necessary to protect American taxpayers': fiscal effects are modest, and where they are not, cheaper keyhole remedies exist (entry fees, surtaxes, exclusion from benefits).
authors.object: Future entrants under open borders; the welfare of migrants and the world as well as natives.

closest.why: No setting of this ledger represents his claim, so no number is shown. His large gains accrue mainly to the migrants themselves (the second row of the table above), and his keyhole remedy applies to future entrants: it cannot be applied to a resident population that is mostly US-born citizens. Switching benefits off in this ledger would only stop counting 364 bn of costs; it would not be his argument.

leaves_out: School, shelter and service load on state and local budgets: what survives a welfare exclusion (audit :288). The audit's verdict on the taxpayer claim: 'Federal gains can coexist with state/local costs in education, shelter, and related services'.
The cost and feasibility of the keyhole instruments themselves (audit :216).

authors.name: Nicholas Decker
argues: 'Immigrants must make us richer': "I think the assumption of constant returns to scale is nonsense... There are three main channels by which returns simply have to be increasing: specialization, ideas, and fixed costs".
authors.object: All immigrants; the aggregate income of incumbents; no horizon or cost convention stated.

closest.why: His argument has a production side and no fiscal side. But this ledger's production block has constant returns, the assumption he rejects, so its near-zero private gain is this account's result and not a test of his claim. The repo has withdrawn two of its own earlier rebuttals of him.

leaves_out: Every fiscal line: the audits record him compressing the question into 'one production-function dispute' (audit 2026-04-11 :255-256).
Composition: his July 2026 visa-ranking proposal concedes that composition decides the sign (scorecard :79).
